questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The electric field inside a good conductor
questions.learningObjective: state that charges redistribute to cancel the field inside a conductor
questions.stem: A steady current is flowing through a copper conductor. What is the electric field like inside the metal itself?

options.text: Zero, because the free charges rearrange until it is cancelled exactly
Nonzero and steady, since a current needs a field to drive it along the wire
options.misconception: applies the driving field at the surface to the interior as well

options.text: Nonzero and rising steadily, since the resistance is turning energy into heat
options.misconception: confuses a growing temperature with a growing interior field

options.text: Zero only at the surface, since the interior is screened from the field
options.misconception: believes screening stops at the surface, leaving the interior conducting

questions.explanation: Free electrons in a metal respond to any field almost instantly, on a timescale of picoseconds, and they redistribute themselves until their own field exactly cancels whatever was applied. What is left inside is nothing, and the current is carried instead by whatever surface charge arrangement sustains that cancellation. This is why the field that drives a current lives on the surface and in the resistive part of a circuit rather than in the good conductors, and why an ideal conducting wire can be treated as a surface rather than as a body when setting up a problem. A steady resistive element is the exception, and it is exactly the part that has a field inside it.
questions.hint: Ask how quickly the free charges can move compared with how quickly the field is applied.

questions.topic: Field components at a boundary between two media
questions.learningObjective: state which component of the field is continuous at a boundary with no free charge
questions.stem: Two dielectric media meet along a plane, with no free charge anywhere on the boundary between them. Which statement about the electric field there is correct?

options.text: The component along the boundary is the same on both sides, while the normal one may jump
Both components are the same on both sides, since a field is continuous everywhere
options.misconception: assumes full continuity, which holds only when the permittivities agree

options.text: The component across the boundary is the same, while the component along it may jump
options.misconception: swaps the roles of the two components, inverting which one is pinned

options.text: Both components may jump, since each medium is set by its own permittivity alone
options.misconception: lets both components jump, overlooking the two continuity conditions

questions.explanation: Shrink a tiny rectangular loop around the boundary so that two of its sides lie along the boundary and two lie across it, and the circulation of the field around that loop tends to zero, which forces the field component along the boundary to be the same on the two sides. The component across the boundary is not pinned, because the amount of charge that can pile up on the interface is set by the two permittivities, and the field just inside a medium of permittivity 4.0 is a quarter of the field just outside for the same surface charge. Those two conditions are the starting point for working out reflection and refraction at any boundary, including the metal surface in the next few items.
questions.hint: Use the field around a vanishingly small loop that straddles the boundary, and see which orientation it forces to match.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a field cannot simply end on a conducting surface
questions.learningObjective: explain that the field outside a conductor is finite and is held there by surface charge
questions.stem: In a sketch of the field around a charged conductor, one field line is drawn running straight into the surface and simply stopping there. What is wrong with that drawing?

options.text: The line has to continue past the surface, since a field cannot end on a boundary
Nothing, because charge on the surface is free to absorb the line where it arrives
options.misconception: assumes surface charge swallows the flux, though the field there is finite

options.text: The line should be doubled so the pattern near the surface looks balanced
options.misconception: tries to balance the pattern by adding a line rather than continuing the existing one

options.text: The line is fine, since a field simply stops at the surface of any material
options.misconception: believes no field can enter a conductor, ignoring the surface charge that supports it

questions.explanation: The field just outside a conductor is perpendicular to the surface and perfectly finite, and it does not rise without limit as the surface is approached, so it cannot be consuming field lines on the way in. What happens instead is that the field is discontinuous there: finite just outside, zero just inside, in a perfect conductor. That step is held in place by the surface charge itself, and the size of the field outside is fixed by that charge divided by the permittivity, so the lines are supported by the boundary rather than consumed by it. This is the single most useful boundary condition for metals, since it lets a surface charge density be read straight off a field diagram.
questions.hint: Ask whether the field just outside the surface is finite, and what the surface charge is doing there.

questions.topic: Field in the gap between a charged sheet and a plate
questions.learningObjective: calculate a boundary field from the surface charge and cross-check it two ways
questions.stem: A large sheet carrying a uniform charge density of 3.0e-6 C per square metre faces a grounded conducting plate across a gap of 1.0 mm. What is the electric field in that gap, in newtons per coulomb? Take eps_0 = 8.85e-12 F/m and give the number only.
questions.explanation: All of the sheet's charge faces the plate, so the field in the gap is the surface charge density over the permittivity, which is 3.0e-6 over 8.85e-12 and gives 3.39e5 N per C. The image route reaches it differently: a grounded plate is equivalent to an image sheet of opposite charge, so the field in the gap is the sum of two equal contributions, twice the isolated-sheet value of 1.69e5, which is 3.39e5 once more. The capacitance route agrees too, since 0.20 m square plates 1.0 mm apart hold 3.54e-10 F, the charge on them is 1.2e-7 C, the potential is 339 V, and 339 V over 1.0e-3 m is 3.39e5. Using the isolated-sheet value is the classic factor-of-two error, and the plate is exactly what removes the second half.
questions.hint: Divide the surface charge density by the permittivity, then check by doubling the isolated-sheet field.

questions.topic: Direction of the field at a conducting surface
questions.learningObjective: state that a conductor's surface cannot sustain a tangential electric field
questions.stem: Just outside the surface of a conductor that is carrying current, how does the electric field point?

options.text: Perpendicular to the surface, held there by the surface charge on it
Along the surface, since that is the direction the current is going
options.misconception: gives a tangential field, which a conductor's surface cannot sustain

options.text: Perpendicular to the surface, but at 45 degrees to the current in the metal
options.misconception: invents an angle at 45 degrees that no boundary condition produces

options.text: Along the surface, but only where the surface is carrying no current
options.misconception: restricts the tangential field to regions without current, which is not the rule

questions.explanation: A tangential field at the surface of a conductor would drive the free surface charges along it without any limit, so no such field can be sustained, and the only component that survives is the normal one. Its size is then set locally by whatever surface charge is present, divided by the permittivity, which is why the field strength in a diagram of a charged conductor is a direct reading of the surface charge density. The tangential field that actually drives a current lives in the resistive material and in the surface region, not in the ideal conducting surface, and that is the distinction a boundary condition is designed to enforce.
questions.hint: Ask what a tangential field at the surface would do to the free charges sitting there.

questions.topic: Field outside and inside a closed charged box
questions.learningObjective: locate the field of a charge on a hollow closed conductor
questions.stem: A closed hollow metal box is given a net charge, which ends up entirely on its outer surface. A probe is then placed outside the box, and a second probe is placed in the empty cavity. What does each probe measure from that charge?

options.text: The outer probe measures a normal field, and the inner one measures nothing at all
Both probes measure a field, since the field passes straight through the metal
options.misconception: ignores the shielding, treating the metal as transparent to a static field

options.text: The outer probe measures nothing, since the charge has moved to the inner surface
options.misconception: moves the charge inward, whereas excess charge sits on the outside of a hollow shell

options.text: The inner probe measures a normal field, since the charge has moved inward
options.misconception: puts the charge on the inner surface, which needs a charge inside the cavity

questions.explanation: Excess charge on a closed conductor all ends up on the outer surface, and the cavity's inner surface and the metal itself carry none, which is what the enclosed-charge law demands. The outer surface charge produces a normal field just outside the box, and a closed surface drawn within the metal, surrounding the cavity, encloses no charge at all, so the field there is zero and so is the field in the cavity. This is why a metal enclosure is a good electrostatic shield, and it is the same zero-flux result that shows up in the companion item about the bore of a charged pipe. The field is not weakened by the metal, it is absent from the cavity altogether.
questions.hint: Draw a closed surface inside the metal, between the walls and the cavity, and count the charge it encloses.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Which field statements hold at a metal surface
questions.learningObjective: identify the field boundary conditions that hold for a good conductor
questions.stem: A plane wave meets the flat surface of a good conductor. Which of the statements about the fields at that surface are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The electric field at the surface stands perpendicular to it, never parallel
The magnetic field at the surface runs parallel to it, never perpendicular
The electric field just inside a good conductor is zero
The magnetic field just inside a good conductor is zero as well
options.misconception: extends the electric shielding to the magnetic field, which does penetrate a conductor

questions.explanation: A good conductor screens an electric field completely, because the free charges in it move to cancel whatever is applied, so the interior electric field is zero and the exterior one must be perpendicular to the surface. A magnetic field is a different matter, since the currents that would cancel a changing magnetic field are themselves limited by the resistance of the metal, so the field penetrates to a finite depth that shrinks as the frequency rises. The magnetic field at the surface is parallel to it rather than perpendicular, because a field ending on a surface has to be accounted for by a current running along that surface, and those surface currents are exactly what a reflecting wave sets up. A static magnetic field would penetrate a conductor altogether, since nothing is changing and no currents are needed to sustain it.
questions.hint: Ask separately whether the electric and magnetic fields can be cancelled inside the metal, and in which direction each one must run at the surface.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Phase of the wave reflected from a conductor
questions.learningObjective: state that reflection from a conductor reverses the field by half a cycle
questions.stem: A plane wave meets a good conductor at normal incidence. What phase does the electric field of the returning wave have relative to the arriving one?

options.text: Reversed by half a cycle, so the two cancel at the surface and peak a quarter wavelength away
Unchanged, so the two add at the surface and cancel a quarter wavelength away
options.misconception: ignores the half-cycle reversal and puts the antinode at the surface

options.text: Reversed by a quarter cycle, so the two arrive in step at the surface
options.misconception: gets the phase shift wrong by a quarter of a cycle rather than a half

options.text: Unchanged, so the two reinforce one another everywhere along the pattern
options.misconception: assumes the incident and reflected waves stay in step, so no pattern forms

questions.explanation: The field has to be zero at the surface of a perfect conductor, and it could not be zero there if the two contributions arrived in step, so the reversal is a half cycle. With that reversal the sum is zero at the surface, largest a quarter of a wavelength away, zero again at half a wavelength, and so on, which is a standing pattern rather than a travelling wave. The magnetic field behaves oppositely, being largest right at the surface, because the two magnetic contributions there are in step while the electric ones are opposed. The half-cycle reversal is also what turns the incident energy back rather than letting it pass through, so it is the mechanism behind reflection and not merely a detail of the standing-wave picture.
questions.hint: Decide what the field must be at the surface, and work backwards from that to the required phase shift.

questions.topic: Field at a surface reflecting a wave
questions.learningObjective: add the incident and reflected fields at a conducting surface
questions.stem: A plane wave in vacuum has a peak electric field of 4.0e2 V per metre and meets a large flat conductor at normal incidence. What is the peak electric field at the conductor's surface, in volts per metre? Take c = 3.0e8 m per second.

options.text: 8.0e2 V per metre, where the two fields are in step at the surface
0 V per metre, since no field at all can exist at a conductor's surface
options.misconception: confuses a very large field with no field, missing the charges that hold it

options.text: 4.0e2 V per metre, since reflection leaves the arriving wave unchanged there
options.misconception: believes reflection does nothing to the field at the point of arrival

options.text: 2.0e2 V per metre, from cancelling the arriving and returning fields
options.misconception: halves the amplitude, as though the reversal removed half of it

questions.explanation: The reflected wave has the same peak amplitude, 4.0e2 V per metre, reversed in phase by half a cycle, and that reversal is already included in its sign, so at the surface the two contributions add and give 8.0e2 V per metre. The standing-wave form confirms it: the total is twice the incident peak times the cosine of the position, and at the surface the cosine is one, so the answer is 2 times 4.0e2, which is 8.0e2. A quarter of a wavelength away, which is 1.5e-2 m for this 6.0 cm wavelength, the cosine is zero and the field vanishes entirely. The magnetic field runs the other way and is at its largest at the surface, where its peak is 1.33e-6 T.
questions.hint: Add the incident and reflected amplitudes at the surface, using the standing-wave form as a check.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a standing pattern settles between two reflectors
questions.learningObjective: explain that two coherent counter-travelling waves give a fixed pattern
questions.stem: A wave bounces between two parallel reflecting surfaces 0.12 m apart. Why does the field between them settle into a fixed pattern of nodes and antinodes rather than a jumble?

options.text: The two travelling waves share a frequency and a fixed phase, so their sum is fixed
The waves interfere randomly, and the pattern only settles by chance over a long time
options.misconception: treats the interference as random when both waves share one frequency

options.text: The surfaces absorb the returning wave, so no pattern can form between them at all
options.misconception: assumes perfect reflectors absorb, which would remove the second wave

options.text: The gap holds a single travelling wave that happens to vary in strength along it
options.misconception: misses that the field in the gap is the sum of two waves running opposite ways

questions.explanation: The gap contains two waves of exactly the same frequency and wavelength, running in opposite directions with a phase relationship set by the path each has travelled, and two such waves add to a standing pattern rather than to another wave. The node and antinode positions are fixed for as long as the excitation lasts, and no energy is carried along the gap even though energy is certainly flowing in at one end and being fed back at the other. The 0.12 m separation fixes which wavelengths will fit at all, since the gap has to contain a whole number of half wavelengths, and that is the condition a resonator is designed around. A single travelling wave varying in strength along the gap would carry energy away, which the pattern here does not.
questions.hint: Ask how many waves are present in the gap and whether their frequencies and phases are fixed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a high-frequency current stays near the surface
questions.learningObjective: explain that a changing field drives screening currents near the surface of a conductor
questions.stem: An alternating current flows in a copper wire at 1.0 MHz. How is that current distributed across the wire's cross-section?

options.text: Confined to a thin layer at the surface, of thickness set by the frequency
Spread evenly across the whole cross-section, exactly as with direct current
options.misconception: assumes the distribution is frequency-independent, which skin effect denies

options.text: Confined to the middle of the wire, where the resistance is lowest
options.misconception: puts the current at the centre, the opposite of what screening achieves

options.text: Confined to a thin layer at the surface, of thickness set by the current
options.misconception: makes the layer thickness depend on current rather than on frequency

questions.explanation: The changing magnetic field inside the metal drives currents in closed loops near the surface, and those screening currents cancel the field over most of the interior, leaving only a thin layer at the surface to carry the real current. The thickness of that layer is the skin depth, which shrinks as the square root of the frequency. At 1.0 MHz in copper the skin depth is 6.50e-5 m, so a wire of radius 1.0 mm carries its current in about 6.5 per cent of its cross-sectional area, and the resistance is 15.4 times the direct-current value. The effect is negligible at mains frequency and dominant at radio frequencies, which is why coils lose their top octave.
questions.hint: Ask what the changing field inside the metal itself induces, and where those induced currents have to flow.

questions.topic: Skin depth in copper at a low frequency
questions.learningObjective: calculate a skin depth and confirm it against the exact field solution
questions.stem: Copper has a conductivity of 5.8e7 S per metre. What is its skin depth at 1.0 kHz, in metres? Take mu_0 = 1.3e-6 H/m and pi = 3.14159, and give the number only.
questions.explanation: The skin depth is one over the square root of pi times the frequency times the permeability times the conductivity, and the product of the last two is 1.3e-6 times 5.8e7, which is 75.4, so the denominator is the square root of 3.14159 times 1.0e3 times 75.4, that is the square root of 2.3687e5, which is 486.7, and 1 over 486.7 is 2.05e-3 m. Solving the full pair of field equations for the decay constant rather than assuming the good-conductor limit returns 2.05e-3 m to five figures, because the displacement current in copper at this frequency is utterly negligible. The same expression at 1.0 MHz gives 6.50e-5 m, 31.6 times smaller, which is the square-root-of-frequency behaviour that the next item isolates.
questions.hint: Take the inverse square root of pi times frequency times permeability times conductivity.

questions.topic: How skin depth scales with frequency
questions.learningObjective: state that skin depth varies as the inverse square root of frequency
questions.stem: The skin depth in a conductor is measured as 65.0 micrometres at 1.0 MHz. What happens to it if the frequency is raised a thousandfold with the material unchanged?

options.text: It falls by the square root of a thousand, so it becomes about 2.06 micrometres
It falls by a thousand, so it becomes 0.065 micrometres
options.misconception: makes the depth inversely proportional to frequency, forgetting the square root

options.text: It falls by a million, so it becomes 0.000065 micrometres
options.misconception: applies the square rather than the square root, exaggerating the fall a thousandfold

options.text: It is unchanged, since the skin depth is set by the material alone
options.misconception: believes the depth has no frequency dependence at all

questions.explanation: Frequency sits under a square root in the expression for skin depth, so raising it a thousandfold divides the depth by the square root of a thousand, which is 31.6, taking 65.0 micrometres to 2.06 micrometres, and the expression evaluated at 1.0 GHz returns 2.05e-6 m, the same figure. The other two quantities in that expression, the conductivity and the permeability, also sit under square roots, so a less conducting material has a deeper skin at a given frequency. Frequency is the practical lever precisely because it is by far the easiest of the three to change, which is why the same piece of wire behaves differently at different radio frequencies without anything being altered.
questions.hint: Locate the frequency in the expression and see what power of it appears.

questions.topic: How much of a wire's cross-section carries a high-frequency current
questions.learningObjective: find the fraction of a cross-section that carries current at a given frequency
questions.stem: A copper wire of radius 1.0 mm carries current at 1.0 MHz. What fraction of its cross-sectional area actually carries that current? Take mu_0 = 1.3e-6 H/m, a conductivity of 5.8e7 S per metre and pi = 3.14159.

options.text: About 6.5 per cent, from the ratio of the skin depth to the wire radius
About 12.6 per cent, from treating the skin layer as a plain uniform annulus
options.misconception: treats the skin layer as uniform, though the density falls off exponentially

options.text: About 3.3 per cent, from halving the skin depth before taking the ratio
options.misconception: halves the depth, confusing the density's exponential fall with the depth

options.text: About 100 per cent, since the whole cross-section is copper and carries some current
options.misconception: treats a vanishingly small interior density as though it were zero everywhere

Treating the layer as a plain uniform annulus out to one skin depth would instead give 12.6 per cent, exactly double the right answer, which is the standard error here. The practical consequence is a resistance 15.4 times the direct-current value for the same wire.
questions.hint: Compare the effective area, pi a times the skin depth, with the full area, pi a squared.

questions.topic: Why a waveguide has a cutoff frequency
questions.learningObjective: explain that a guide's field pattern sets a minimum wavelength
questions.stem: A hollow rectangular metal pipe is used to carry microwaves. Why is there a lowest frequency below which nothing gets through?

options.text: A field pattern has to fit between the walls, which sets a minimum wavelength
There is none, since the inside is empty and carries whatever a vacuum carries
options.misconception: assumes the walls add nothing, ignoring the boundary conditions they impose

options.text: It comes from the resistance of the walls, which grows as the frequency rises
options.misconception: makes the cutoff a resistive effect, though the walls are treated as perfect

options.misconception: misplaces the decimal in the propagation time and then rescales the cycle count

questions.topic: A quarter-wave section as an impedance transformer

options.text: It presents the load divided by the line impedance, a ratio rather than a square

options.text: It presents the reciprocal of the load impedance, as any passive section must
options.misconception: insists on reciprocity, which constrains power and not impedance

questions.explanation: Aperture and directivity are the same quantity read in two directions, since the effective aperture is the directivity times the wavelength squared over 4 pi, so for a fixed wavelength a dish twice as wide in both directions has four times the area, four times the directivity, and therefore collects or radiates four times as much in its best direction. The total power is unchanged, so all of that extra has to come out of the directions outside the beam, and the beam narrows as a direct consequence. A half-wave dipole at 1.00 m has an effective aperture of 0.131 square metres from a directivity of 1.64, while an ideal radiator has 0.0796, which is the factor of about 1.64 by which it wins in its best direction.
questions.hint: Look for the single relationship that links aperture, directivity and the concentration of power.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: The chain from transmitted power to a detected echo
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps in a radar detection chain
questions.stem: Four steps describe the chain from a radar transmitter to a detected echo. Put them in the order in which they occur.

options.text: Spread that density over the sphere at the target's range to get the outgoing density
Multiply the transmitted power by the antenna gain to get the power radiated
Multiply the returning density by the target's effective area to get the power it reradiates
Spread that reradiated power over a second sphere to get the density at the receiver

questions.explanation: The chain starts at the feed, where the gain turns the transmitter's power into the power actually radiated, and from there every later step is a spreading loss of one kind or another. The outgoing density at the target is that power over the area of the sphere at the target's range, which is the first inverse square. The target then does what any scatterer does, intercepting a fixed fraction of that density over its effective area and reradiating it, which is the step that introduces the target's radar cross-section. Finally that reradiated power spreads over a second sphere of the same radius, and the result is the second inverse square, which is what turns an inverse square into an inverse fourth power.
questions.hint: The order runs from the feed outwards, through the target, and back to the receiver.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Why a reflected wave is the mirror image of the incident one
questions.learningObjective: explain the phase reversal at a conducting surface from the field boundary condition
questions.stem: A wave meets a metal surface and comes back apparently upside down. Explain in your own words why a conductor must reverse the phase of the field, and what that reversal produces.

answer.exemplar: Start from the boundary condition rather than from the picture. Inside a good conductor the electric field is zero, because the free charges move fast enough to cancel whatever is applied, and that cancellation takes picoseconds rather than any appreciable time. The field therefore has to be zero at the surface itself, not just a short distance in. Now the arriving wave and the returning wave both have fields at that surface, and the condition can only be met if they are equal in size and opposite in sign, so the returning electric field must be reversed by half a cycle. Nothing arbitrary is happening: the surface charges have to arrange themselves into whatever pattern is needed, and the field they produce is exactly the missing half of the cancellation. The magnetic field behaves oppositely, because a magnetic field cannot be cancelled by charge moving freely, since that motion is what produces it in the first place; the surface currents instead arrange to reinforce the arriving magnetic field, so the two magnetic contributions are in step at the surface and the magnetic field is at its maximum there. The pair of conditions is what produces the standing pattern. The electric field is zero at the surface and largest a quarter of a wavelength away, zero again at half a wavelength, and so on along the guide or the gap, while the magnetic field runs a quarter of a wavelength out of step with it. For an incident peak of 4.0e2 volts per metre the surface electric field is 8.0e2, since the two in-step contributions add there, and the whole pattern repeats every half wavelength. That the field vanishes at the surface while the surface current is at its maximum is also the physical statement that the conductor is absorbing no energy: the current is there to hold the condition, and it is fed by the wave, not by the surface charge itself.

questions.explanation: The electric field must be zero at a conductor's surface, so the arriving and returning electric fields are equal and opposite there, which is a half-cycle reversal, while the magnetic field is reinforced instead and is largest at the surface.
questions.hint: Begin with the requirement that the electric field vanish at the surface, and let the phase reversal follow from it.

questions.topic: Choosing the two data a propagation calculation needs
questions.learningObjective: identify the frequency and geometry that fix a guide's behaviour
questions.stem: A guide of broad internal dimension 3.00 cm is to be used at some frequency the user has not yet fixed. First say what sets its cutoff, then say what the user must also fix before any guide wavelength can be quoted.

options.text: The broad dimension sets the cutoff, and the user must fix the running frequency
The frequency sets the cutoff, and the user must fix the broad dimension
options.misconception: has the two roles exchanged, so neither step leads to the right geometry

options.text: The conductivity of the walls sets the cutoff, and the user must fix the length
options.misconception: brings in a wall property that does not enter the cutoff at all

options.text: The narrow dimension sets the cutoff, and the user must fix the guide length
options.misconception: uses the narrow dimension, which belongs to the higher modes only

questions.explanation: The cutoff is fixed by the guide's own geometry, the speed of light over twice the broad dimension, so 3.00e8 over 0.060, which is 5.00e9 Hz, and nothing the user chooses at the far end of the system can move it. The guide wavelength, on the other hand, is the free-space wavelength at whatever frequency is in use divided by the square root of 1 minus the square of the cutoff ratio, and it needs both that frequency and the cutoff, so with the cutoff already known from the geometry, the frequency is the missing input. It is also the input that decides whether a mode propagates at all, so a figure quoted without it is not merely incomplete but ambiguous between propagating and decaying.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two inputs is fixed by the hardware and which has to be supplied by the user.
